status: BOOTSTRAP — structural scaffold only. Tiers, membership, controls and chokepoints are analytically derived. Every numeric field is a placeholder prior and MUST be replaced by interest-researcher with sourced values before any run is treated as evidence. Runs on this file unmodified are illustrative of the machinery, not of the world.

conventions.exit_cost_of_using_leverage: 0-1. How much the actor destroys of its own position by actually firing its weapon. High = leverage exists on paper only.
conventions.time_horizon_years: Derived from the selection cycle, not from stated strategy documents.
conventions.shadgunya_default: Kautilyan posture: sandhi | vigraha | asana | yana | samshraya | dvaidhibhava
conventions.mandala_role: From a named vijigishu frame: ari | mitra | madhyama | udasina

actors.label: United States (executive + Congress + security state)
actors.selectorate: national electorate via EC, Senate, donor class, security establishment
actors.notes: Split actor under stress: model as 2 factions if legitimacy < 0.45. Sanctions reach degrades with use — each application accelerates counterparty exit.

actors.label: China (party-state)
actors.selectorate: Politburo Standing Committee, ~200 Central Committee, PLA leadership
actors.notes: Longest horizon of any T1 actor — this asymmetry is structurally decisive against 2-4 year democracies. Binding constraints are demographic, property-balance-sheet and food/energy import dependence, not political.

actors.label: EU core (DE/FR/NL + Commission)
actors.selectorate: national electorates + Council unanimity + Commission technocracy
actors.notes: Highest exit cost of any major bloc: unanimity means leverage is real but slow and rarely fired. Energy import dependence is the binding constraint. Candidate for splitting into northern-creditor and southern-debtor actors under fiscal stress.

actors.label: India (union government)
actors.selectorate: national electorate, state coalition partners, business houses
actors.notes: Classic Kautilyan madhyama — can tip either bloc and is paid by both for doing so. Binding constraints: energy import bill, current account, employment absorption. The hedging premium is the asset; anything that forces a side-choice destroys it.

actors.label: Japan + South Korea (advanced allied manufacturers)
actors.selectorate: national electorates + keiretsu/chaebol + US alliance dependence
actors.notes: Merged on shared constraint: US security dependence, China trade dependence, severe demographics, creditor status. Diverge on China exposure — split if Taiwan conflict_index > 0.6.

actors.label: Taiwan
actors.selectorate: national electorate; effectively also US policy
actors.notes: Not merged despite small size: sole holder of the single most concentrated chokepoint in the system. Exit cost ~1.0 — its leverage cannot be fired without self-destruction, which makes it a hostage rather than a wielder. The silicon shield is a deterrent to others, not a weapon for it.

actors.label: Russia
actors.selectorate: presidential inner circle, siloviki, resource oligarchy
actors.notes: Low exit cost — already sanctioned, so marginal cost of further leverage use is small. This is the general rule: an actor with little left to lose is a cheap escalator. Variance-preferring by position.

actors.label: Gulf petro-monarchies (SA, UAE, QA)
actors.selectorate: ruling families, succession politics
actors.notes: Merged on shared fiscal breakeven logic and dynastic succession structure. Long horizon from non-electoral selection. Uniquely positioned as both commodity chokepoint and capital allocator — appears in T1 and, via SWF, in T2.

actors.label: Atlantic financial entrepôts (UK, IE, LU)
actors.selectorate: domestic electorates + financial sector capture + alliance alignment
actors.notes: SPLIT from ST_ENTREPOT (2026-09) on sourced evidence: weaponization-willing, coordinated with US/EU sanctions architecture. UK committed GBP2.26bn to the G7 reparations-loan structure fastest and most eagerly of any entrepot.

actors.label: Neutrality-preserving entrepôts (CH, SG, HK-uncertain)
actors.selectorate: domestic electorates + financial sector capture + host-state tolerance
actors.notes: SPLIT from ST_ENTREPOT (2026-09) on sourced evidence: neutrality franchise is real but eroding (2026 Swiss parliamentary confiscation-measures endorsement). Singapore/HK positioning not directly sourced -- inherited low-confidence flag, not resolved.

actors.label: Swing middle powers (BR, ID, MX, TR, VN, ZA, SA-region)
actors.selectorate: national electorates, militaries, commodity and manufacturing elites
actors.notes: Merged on shared strategy — sell alignment to both blocs and refuse to choose — not on geography. Principal beneficiaries of bifurcation. Split into regional actors if a run turns on one of them specifically.

actors.label: FX-constrained frontier debtors (EG, PK, KE, AR, NG, LK-type)
actors.selectorate: urban constituencies, militaries, IMF and bilateral creditors
actors.notes: Shortest horizon, tightest liquidity constraint, most frequent regime breaks. The tier's shock transmitter: their defaults and migration surges are the mechanism by which distress reaches T1 core actors. Never omit for tidiness.

actors.label: US Federal Reserve
actors.selectorate: Board + FOMC + Senate confirmation + implicit executive pressure
actors.notes: Swap-line allocation is the single most underrated political instrument in the system: a discretionary, near-instant decision on who survives a dollar squeeze. Independence is itself a Kautilyan commitment device — delegation to an actor with different preferences. Model divergence from ST_US explicitly; it matters most exactly when it appears.

actors.label: European Central Bank
actors.selectorate: Governing Council, national central banks, treaty mandate
actors.notes: Uniquely constrained: single monetary authority, no single fiscal counterpart. The fragmentation backstop is a commitment device whose credibility has never been fully tested at scale.

actors.label: People's Bank of China
actors.selectorate: State Council — not independent
actors.notes: Faces the impossible-trinity trade-off most sharply. Reserve-currency ambition requires capital account opening, which surrenders the control that makes the system governable. That tension is a primary generator of branch points.

actors.label: Bank of Japan
actors.selectorate: Policy Board, MoF coordination
actors.notes: Largest creditor position in the system. Japanese rate normalisation repatriates capital and is a global transmission event far out of proportion to Japan's GDP share. A recurring, under-modelled branch point.

actors.label: Reserve Bank of India
actors.selectorate: MPC + government appointment
actors.notes: Manages the classic EM trilemma with a large reserve buffer. UPI is an emerging strategic asset — a domestically controlled payment rail exportable to partner states, a genuine sovereignty instrument.

actors.label: EM central bank bloc (BR, ID, TR, ZA, MX, GCC pegs)
actors.selectorate: national governments with varying degrees of formal independence
actors.notes: Price-takers on global dollar conditions. Their collective reserve-composition shift is the actual mechanism of any de-dollarisation, so track it as a flow rather than reading the rhetoric.

actors.label: Sovereign wealth funds (NBIM, PIF, ADIA, GIC, Temasek, CIC)
actors.selectorate: sponsoring states
actors.notes: Longest horizon of any capital actor in the system. Structurally advantaged against quarterly-reporting competitors — the purest example of horizon arbitrage available, and the clearest template for what the OBS seat is trying to imitate.

actors.label: Multilateral institutions (IMF, World Bank, BIS, regional MDBs)
actors.selectorate: weighted shareholder votes — US veto at IMF
actors.notes: Shareholding makes this a near-proxy for ST_US at decision points, but it is NOT merged: it acts through a conditionality mechanism with its own logic, and the divergence from its principal is informative.

actors.label: Index complex (BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street, index providers)
actors.selectorate: asset-owner clients, index methodology committees
actors.notes: The most important mechanical actor in the system and the most rule-bound. Index inclusion and exclusion decisions move national costs of capital and are made by small committees. Its mandate rigidity is the primary source of constraint arbitrage for OBS: it MUST buy and sell on rules, regardless of price.

actors.label: Active managers, pensions, endowments, insurers-as-investors
actors.selectorate: trustees, beneficiaries, regulators
actors.notes: Heavily constrained by liability matching, solvency rules and benchmark risk. Pension demand for long duration is a forced flow — mechanically certain and frequently mispriced.

actors.label: US-chartered globally systemic banks
actors.selectorate: shareholders + boards + prudential regulators + implicit sovereign backstop
actors.notes: SPLIT from BANK_GSIB (2026-09) on sourced evidence: national regulators ring-fence in a crisis, confirmed by 2023 divergence. US FDIC's systemic-risk exception covered only US-chartered deposits, funded domestically -- self-protective, jurisdiction-first.

actors.label: Non-US globally systemic banks (EU, UK, CH, JP, CN majors)
actors.selectorate: shareholders + boards + prudential regulators + implicit sovereign backstop
actors.notes: SPLIT from BANK_GSIB (2026-09). Internally heterogeneous, not a coordinated bloc: Switzerland unilaterally inverted its AT1/equity creditor waterfall in 2023 while the EU and BoE explicitly repudiated that approach for their own jurisdictions within days -- three different positions in one fortnight.

actors.label: Private credit, PE, and shadow banks (Blackstone, Apollo, KKR, Ares)
actors.selectorate: LPs, fund economics
actors.notes: Fastest-growing and least-observed part of the credit system. Mark discretion means its stress is invisible until it is acute — a structural monitoring gap and therefore a likely site of surprise.

actors.label: Hedge funds, prop trading, market makers (Citadel, Jane Street, Millennium, CTAs)
actors.selectorate: investors, internal risk limits
actors.notes: Variance-preferring: payoffs rise with volatility regardless of direction. Lowest exit cost of any T3 actor — can act without institutional consequence. Withdrawal of liquidity precisely when it is most needed is a feature of the business model, not a failure of it.

actors.label: Exchanges, CCPs and settlement (DTCC, LCH, CME, Euroclear, CLS, SWIFT)
actors.selectorate: member firms, boards, regulators
actors.notes: The plumbing. Euroclear's immobilisation of Russian reserves demonstrated that custody is a weapon, and every reserve manager on earth updated on it. A margin-requirement change is a monetary-policy-scale event executed by a private risk committee with no public mandate.

actors.label: Insurers and reinsurers (Munich Re, Swiss Re, Lloyd's, P&I clubs)
actors.selectorate: shareholders, syndicates, regulators
actors.notes: An uninsurable route is a closed route. This tier can shut a strait without a single warship, and war-risk premia are the cleanest publicly observable conflict forecast available — a market of people with money at stake, priced daily.

actors.label: Semiconductor complex (TSMC, ASML, Samsung, AMAT, Tokyo Electron, NVIDIA)
actors.selectorate: shareholders, host-state export control regimes
actors.notes: The tightest chokepoint in the system: single-digit supplier counts at several layers. But exit cost is very high — these firms cannot fire their own leverage, only host states can fire it for them. Capability held hostage by jurisdiction.

actors.label: Energy majors and NOCs (Aramco, ADNOC, Exxon, Shell, CNPC, Petrobras)
actors.selectorate: shareholders or sponsoring states
actors.notes: Underinvestment is itself a strategic action with a 5-10 year delayed payoff. Refining configuration — who can process which crude grade — is a persistently under-modelled chokepoint and explains much of the sanctions-evasion geography.

actors.label: Hyperscalers and AI labs (MSFT, GOOG, AMZN, META, NVDA, OpenAI, Anthropic)
actors.selectorate: shareholders, founders with control stock, regulators
actors.notes: Capex here is now macro-relevant in its own right — large enough to move national accounts and global rates. Also the only T3 actor with direct influence over T4 belief formation, which gives it a legitimacy channel no other capital actor has.

actors.label: Physical commodity traders (Vitol, Trafigura, Glencore, Cargill, ADM, COFCO)
actors.selectorate: private partners, shareholders, banking syndicates
actors.notes: The actors who actually move the goods, and they are private, opaque and rarely in any model. Profit directly from dislocation and sanction, which makes them structurally variance-preferring. Reroute flows faster than states can legislate.

actors.label: Defence industrial base (LMT, RTX, BAE, Rheinmetall, NORINCO, HAL)
actors.selectorate: shareholders + sponsoring states as monopsony buyer
actors.notes: Multi-year procurement backlogs are the most reliable public statement of a state's real intent — expensive, slow to reverse, and visible. Track order books, not white papers.

actors.label: Asset-owning households, developed markets
actors.notes: Politically decisive in most DM systems and structurally opposed to inflation and to asset-price declines. Their preference is the real constraint behind central bank reaction functions, whatever the mandate says.

actors.label: Wage-dependent households, developed markets
actors.notes: The consent constraint on T1. Withdrawal shows up as populist realignment with a 2-4 round lag — slow, lumpy, and then abrupt. Real wage growth versus asset prices is the leading indicator worth tracking.

actors.label: Chinese households
actors.notes: Financially repressed, property-concentrated, few outbound options. Their savings fund the system's investment; any shift in that behaviour transmits globally through the current account. Low voice, high structural weight.

actors.label: Indian households
actors.notes: Gold holdings function as a private, decentralised FX reserve outside state control — a genuine and under-modelled buffer. The domestic SIP bid has become structurally significant to local equity pricing and is a forced flow worth tracking.

actors.label: EM urban middle class
actors.notes: Dollarisation by households is the fastest and most reliable early warning of currency regime failure, and it moves before any official statistic does.

actors.label: Subsistence and informal households
actors.notes: Highest exit cost, shortest horizon, least voice — and the tier that bears the transition. Food and fuel prices are the transmission channel from global markets to regime change, historically the most reliable in the entire system. Never drop this actor.

actors.label: Organised labour and professional guilds
actors.selectorate: membership
actors.notes: Weak in aggregate, decisive at specific chokepoints. A few thousand port or rail workers can halt more trade than most sanctions regimes.

no material action capability; useful only as a cheap-talk alignment readout
not actors with distinct utility — model as endogenous coalitions among existing T1 actors
largely mechanical given observable data; their downgrades are a trigger mechanism, not a choice
no agency; enters via the shock table with rising and correlated frequency
model as an endogenous coalition of ST_GULF + ST_RU with an explicit core-stability check each round
currently a T3 sub-actor within NBFI_CREDIT; promote to its own actor if stablecoin holdings of T-bills exceed a material share of the bill market, or if it becomes a primary sanctions-evasion rail

chokepoints: refining and separation capacity, not ore

proposed_theatres_NOTE: Historical snapshot from the original Cartographer pass. The live theatre definitions (with kernel assignments) are in theatres.json, which has since diverged from this list -- notably ST_ENTREPOT and BANK_GSIB were split into ST_ENTREPOT_ATLANTIC/NEUTRAL and BANK_GSIB_US/INTL per interest-researcher findings (see open_questions below). Do not treat this array as current.
open_questions: RESOLVED 2026-09: ST_ENTREPOT split into ST_ENTREPOT_ATLANTIC (UK/IE/LU) and ST_ENTREPOT_NEUTRAL (CH/SG/HK-unconfirmed) -- interest-researcher confirmed the divergence with sourced evidence (UK's eager reparations-loan commitment vs Switzerland's 2026 parliamentary reversal on confiscation).
Should CORP_TECH be promoted to T1? Its capex is macro-scale and its compute allocation is arguably a sovereign-grade chokepoint.
Does ST_EU survive as a single actor through a fiscal stress episode, or split into northern-creditor and southern-debtor actors?
Is stablecoin-held T-bill demand already material enough to promote crypto out of NBFI_CREDIT?
ST_TW exit cost is near 1.0 — does it belong as an actor at all, or as a contested asset in the taiwan_semiconductor theatre?
Are HH_CN and HH_IN doing enough distinct work to justify two actors, or should they merge into a single high-savings-EM-household actor?
